# King's Scholar
The title "King's Scholar" originated in 1317 under King Edward II at the University of Cambridge and was institutionalized at various historic English schools, notably Eton College. At Eton, King's Scholars—colloquially known as "Collegers" or "tugs"—are selected through the College Election examination, awarded a Foundation Scholarship, and housed in the oldest Eton house, "College", within the school's central, historic precincts. Traditionally, there are around 70 King's Scholars, each wearing a distinctive black academic gown. While the scholarship once guaranteed a full fee waiver, since the 1960s it has become subject to means testing, and not all fees may be covered for current scholars. King's Scholars are marked in school lists by the post-nominal "KS"; Oppidan Scholars, attached to other houses, are distinguished only academically.
Collegers share most aspects of school life with other students but have unique privileges, including dining in College Hall and more sustained participation in traditions like the Wall Game. Many notable public figures—such as George Orwell, John Maynard Keynes, and Boris Johnson—were King's Scholars at Eton. The King's Scholar designation is also present at Westminster School (adjusted to Queen's Scholar when a Queen reigns), at King’s College Cambridge for undergraduates obtaining first-class degrees, and at The King's Schools (Canterbury, Chester, Ely, Gloucester, Peterborough, Rochester, Worcester), which award King's Scholarships in recognition of academic or musical attainment and may grant select ceremonial rights, such as privileges at cathedrals. Schools such as King's Ely and King's Worcester have adapted the King's Scholarship for coeducation, and its recognition now can offer fee discounts or other distinctions.
